chapter_theme: In an ascetic's borrowed form Manimekalai hears the schools of Vanji one by one: the Vedic logician's means of knowledge and their fallacies, the Saiva, Brahma, Vaishnava and Vedic accounts of God and scripture, the Ajivika's atoms and fixed fate, the Jain categories and release by exhausting deeds, Sankhya's nature and person, the Vaisheshika categories, and the materialist's denial of any next world, which alone she answers, turning his trust in perception against his knowledge of his own parents. Every school is given in a Buddhist work's account and set aside on the way to the Buddhist teaching of kaathai 29.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, a Buddhist renunciant here going among the schools in an ascetic's borrowed form
the Vedic logician who sets out the means of valid knowledge
the debater for the Saiva view of God
the debater who holds the world to be an egg laid by one god
the reciter of the purana of the sea-coloured god, for Narayana as protector
the Vedic brahmin who holds the Veda to be without beginning or end
the Ajivika teacher, versed in the book of Makkali

manimekalai:27:1-24.unit_note: Boundary moved from 15 to 24: the definition of perception that begins at 14 runs to அறிவது ஆகும் at line 24; the core unit 1-15 broke it mid-list.
manimekalai:27:1-24.reading: Manimekalai goes among the schools' reckoners and asks the Vedic logician his doctrine; he names the teachers who counted ten, eight and six means of knowledge, lists the ten, and defines perception as fivefold sense-knowledge that, free of indefiniteness, error and doubt, grasps a thing's place, name, class, quality and action.
manimekalai:27:1-24.nuance: The logician is called வைதிக மார்க்கத்து அளவை வாதி, and his authorities are Vyasa, Kritakoti and Jaimini, so the school is Vedic without being one darsana; the chapter does not tie him to Nyaya or Mimamsa. Lines 9 to 12 name what reads as eleven items for the ten promised (மீட்சி ஒழிவறிவு may be one item, and உண்டாம் நெறி is the உள்ள நெறி of line 55). The account is given by a Buddhist work and is answered in kaathai 29, where perception is stripped of name, class, quality and action.
manimekalai:27:1-24.event: Manimekalai comes to the Vedic logician and asks him to state his doctrine; he begins to set out the means of knowledge.

claims.claim: the truth of things must be grasped through the means of valid knowledge
valid perception is of five kinds, one for each sense
sound perception grasps a thing's place, name, class, quality and action

manimekalai:27:25-40.unit_note: Starts at 25 where the definition of inference (கருத்து அளவு ஆவது) opens, and ends at 40, which closes the account of inference before உவமம் at 41.
manimekalai:27:25-40.reading: The logician defines inference as knowing the inferable through a mark, in three kinds, and gives an example of each: the unseen elephant known by its sound, rain upstream known by the flood, rain to come known from pregnant clouds; a sound reason, tied to one of the three times and free of fault, knows the unseen through the seen.
manimekalai:27:25-40.nuance: The three kinds (பொது, எச்சம், முதல்) run from present sign, from effect back to cause, and from cause forward to effect. Lines 29 and 30, on the general kind holding even without concomitance (அந்நுவயம் இன்றாய் இருந்தும்), are hard to construe and the reading here is tentative.

claims.claim: inference knows the thing to be inferred through a mark
inference is of three kinds: general, from effect, and from cause
a valid reason, tied to one of the three times and free of fault, knows the unseen through the seen

manimekalai:27:41-56.unit_note: Runs from உவமம் at 41 to line 56, where the last of the ten means (உள்ள நெறி) closes with எனக் கூறல்; the core units broke at 53, inside the example of மீட்சி.
manimekalai:27:41-56.reading: The logician gives the remaining means with an example each: comparison (the wild gavaya is like a cow), scripture (from the knower's book, that a world of enjoyment exists), presumption (a village 'on the Ganga' must be on its bank), aptness (the man on the elephant asking for a goad is handed the goad), tradition (a ghost haunts this tree), absence, implication (Rama won, so Ravana lost), and possibility (what turns an iron rod is a magnet).
manimekalai:27:41-56.nuance: Scripture counts as its own means here, and its example is an unseen world (போக புவனம்): the logician needs it for exactly what perception and inference cannot reach, which is where the Lokayata at the chapter's end will refuse to follow.

claims.claim: comparison is a separate means of knowledge
scripture, the knower's book, gives valid knowledge of unseen worlds
presumption, tradition, absence and the rest are each a means of knowledge in their own right

manimekalai:27:57-85.unit_note: Joins the core units 54-76 (from 57) and 77-89 (to 85): the eight fallacies run from 57 to the middle of 77, and the same sentence goes on (இப் பெற்றிய அளவைகள்) into the list of schools, which ends at 85 before the narrator turns to the Saiva at 86. Lines 54-56 go with the unit before.
manimekalai:27:57-85.reading: The logician lists eight false semblances of knowledge, each with an example (bare awareness that something is there, shell taken for silver, 'post or man?', a post taken for a man without looking, failing to know a tiger seen, the hare's horn, knowing the known, and taking on others' word that these are your parents), then pairs six schools with their teachers and closes that six means of knowledge are current now.
manimekalai:27:57-85.nuance: The list at 78 to 85 sets six schools against six teachers and six means, and is most simply read cumulatively: Lokayata with perception alone, the Buddhists with inference added, and so on to Mimamsa with absence. சினன் (Jina) is here the Buddhists' teacher, as ஆதி சினேந்திரன் is the Buddha at 29:47; it is not the Jain Tirthankara. The parents example at 75 to 77, filed here as a fallacy, is the one Manimekalai turns on the materialist at 284.

claims.claim: there are eight false semblances of valid knowledge
to hold on others' word that these are one's mother and father is memory, a false semblance of knowledge
six means of knowledge, perception to absence, are those current now among the six schools

manimekalai:27:86-95.unit_note: The core unit 77-89 is split: 86 opens with the narrator leaving the logician for the Saiva, and 95 closes the Saiva's speech with என்று உரைத்தனன்.
manimekalai:27:86-95.reading: Leaving the logician, Manimekalai asks the Saiva debater what his god is like; he answers that the Lord is the one who is the eight (the two lights, the sacrificer and the five elements), who binds soul and body, whose form is the arts, who creates and plays, who wipes away sorrow, and who has nothing other than himself.
manimekalai:27:86-95.nuance: இரு சுடரோடு இயமானன் ஐம் பூதம் is the eight-formed god, in the oldest form of the list. தன்னில் வேறு தான் ஒன்று இலோன், the one with nothing other than himself, can be read as sole being or as one beyond any second; the line does not settle which.
manimekalai:27:86-95.event: Manimekalai leaves the logician and asks the Saiva debater what his god is like, and he describes Siva.

claims.claim: God is the one who is the eight forms: sun, moon, the sacrificer and the five elements
God binds the soul to the body, creates the world in play and removes sorrow
God has nothing other than himself

manimekalai:27:96-107.unit_note: The core unit 90-107 is cut at 96, where the Brahma-vadin's speech begins after the Saiva's என்று உரைத்தனன் at 95.
manimekalai:27:96-107.reading: In quick succession the Brahma-vadin says the whole world is an egg laid by one god, a devotee recites the purana of the sea-coloured god and says Narayana protects, and the Vedic brahmin says the Veda, with its six limbs as hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose and face, arises from no cause and has no beginning or end; Manimekalai judges that none of their words agrees with any way of truth.
manimekalai:27:96-107.nuance: The Veda is called சார்பின் தோன்றா, not arising from dependence: in a Buddhist work, whose own teaching is that everything arises by சார்பு, this is the phrase most open to attack. Manimekalai's verdict at 106 to 107 covers the whole group heard since 86 (இவர் உரை), not only the brahmin.
manimekalai:27:96-107.event: The Brahma-vadin, a Vaishnava reciter and a Vedic brahmin state their views, and Manimekalai rejects them all.

claims.claim: the whole world is an egg laid by one god
Narayana is the protector
the Veda with its six limbs arises from no cause and has neither beginning nor end, and it is the path
the words of these speakers agree with no way of truth or accepted usage

manimekalai:27:108-119.reading: Manimekalai asks Puranan, who knows the Ajivika book, for his god and his categories; he says the god is the knower without limit, present in all things at all times, and the categories are five, the soul and four kinds of atom, which touch, are seen, combine into mountain, tree and body and part again, while the soul is what knows.
manimekalai:27:108-119.nuance: புராணன் may be the teacher's name (an Ajivika teacher Purana is known from other traditions) or a description, one learned in the old book; the line allows either. Four kinds of atom without a fifth for space is part of the account as given.
manimekalai:27:108-119.event: Manimekalai asks the Ajivika teacher for his god and his doctrine, and he begins.

claims.claim: the god is the knower without limit, present in all things at all times
there are five categories: the soul and four kinds of atom
atoms combine into mountains, trees and bodies and part again, while the soul is what knows

manimekalai:27:120-141.reading: The Ajivika gives each element's nature (earth hard and low, water cool and sinking, fire burning and rising, wind moving) and says the atoms are without beginning, never destroyed, never newly born, never entering one another or turning into another kind, never splitting or spreading, yet they move, sink and rise, mass into mountains and diamonds, part again, and in a compound are named for the element that predominates.
manimekalai:27:120-141.nuance: The proportions at 140 (one, three quarters, half, quarter) give a rule for naming mixtures by the larger share; the images of bamboo and the unwaning moon at 136 and 137 are examples of what massed atoms become, and their exact sense is not secure.

claims.claim: atoms have no beginning, are never destroyed or newly born, and never change their kind
a compound of atoms is named for the element that predominates in it

manimekalai:27:142-158.unit_note: Ends at 158 instead of 157: the sentence இது தப்பும் அது மண்டலம் என்று அறியல் வேண்டும் runs over 157 into 158.
manimekalai:27:142-158.reading: The Ajivika says atoms act as earth, water, fire or wind only in these qualities; a single atom is seen only by those with divine eyes, as a single hair is not seen at dusk though a mass of hair is; and beings born through six births in order, black, dark blue, green, red, golden and white, reach release in the last white birth, a straight course they cannot fail to reach, while straying from it is the circling round.
manimekalai:27:142-158.nuance: The six colour-births are the Ajivika's own scheme as this account gives it. கருமம் பிறப்பு at 150 is read as the dark birth; பசும்ம், செம்ம், பொன்ன், வெண்ண் have an added consonant as printed. அழியல் வேண்டார் அது உறற்பாலார் says those in the course need not perish and are bound to reach it: release here comes by a fixed course, not by effort.

claims.claim: a single atom is seen only by those with divine sight
beings pass in order through six births by colour and reach release in the last, white birth

manimekalai:27:159-170.unit_note: Moved to 159-170 from the core 158-180: 158 closes the colour-births, 165 closes the Ajivika's speech (மற்கலி நூலின் வகை இது), and 170 closes Manimekalai's question to the Jain, whose answer begins at 171.
manimekalai:27:159-170.reading: The Ajivika ends that gain and loss, hindrance, pleasure and pain, parting, birth and death are all mixed in at the moment of conception, that pleasure and pain are themselves atoms, and that the fate laid down before makes what comes after, which is the doctrine of Makkali's book; Manimekalai leaves this tangle of words and asks the Jain debater for his lord, his categories, how they occur, and bondage and release.
manimekalai:27:159-170.nuance: This is the chapter's strongest statement of fate, and it is put in a rival's mouth: everything a life meets is fixed at conception, with no room for deed or effort. The Buddhist narrator's word for it, சொல் தடுமாற்றத் தொடர்ச்சி, is a dismissal, not an argument.
manimekalai:27:159-170.event: The Ajivika finishes; Manimekalai leaves him and asks the Jain debater to state his doctrine.

claims.claim: gain, loss, pleasure, pain, birth and death are all fixed at the moment of conception
pleasure and pain are themselves atoms
the fate laid down before brings about what comes after

manimekalai:27:171-182.unit_note: The core unit 158-180 is cut at 171, where the Jain's answer begins, and ends at 182, where the sentence on origination, persistence and destruction closes with ஆக்கலும் உரித்தாம்.
manimekalai:27:171-182.reading: The Jain says his lord is the one the Indras worship, and the categories he gave are dharma, adharma, time, space, the faultless soul, atoms, good and bad deeds, the bondage they cause, and release; each thing has its own nature and a nature from what it depends on, is both lasting and passing, and in every moment takes on origination, persistence and destruction.
manimekalai:27:171-182.nuance: Dharma and adharma here are not merit and demerit but the media of motion and rest (as 187 to 190 make clear); merit and demerit are named separately at 175. A thing both lasting and passing is the Jain many-sided view of substance and its modes.

claims.claim: the lord is the one whom the Indras worship
the categories are dharma, adharma, time, space, soul, atoms, merit, demerit, bondage and release
every thing is both lasting and passing, and in each moment originates, persists and is destroyed

manimekalai:27:183-201.unit_note: Runs from 183, where the examples begin, to 201, where the Jain's speech ends with வீடு ஆகும் என்றனன்; the core units broke at 196 and 197, inside the account of the soul and of release.
manimekalai:27:183-201.reading: The Jain illustrates with the sprouting neem and with gram cooked into a dish (the kind persists while the form passes), says dharma pervades all and makes things move, adharma makes them stay, time is the instant and the aeon, space gives room to all, the soul joins a body and enjoys the senses, the atom is matter's outward form, and release is to block the inflow of both good and bad deeds and wear out the fruit of past deeds by living it through.
manimekalai:27:183-201.nuance: Release needs no grace and no god here: it is the stopping of new deeds and the exhausting of old ones. Both good and bad deeds bind (இரண்டையும் மாற்றி). Line 190's number in the source carries the kaathai number (227-190).

claims.claim: dharma pervades all and makes things move; adharma makes them stay
the soul joins a body and through it enjoys the senses
release is to block the inflow of both good and bad deeds and exhaust past deeds by experiencing their fruit

manimekalai:27:202-226.unit_note: Runs from 202, where the Sankhya speaker begins, to 226, where the account of primal nature closes (ஒன்றாய் எங்கும் பரந்து நித்தியம் ஆம்) before the account of purusha at 227; the core units broke at 220 and 221, inside the list of the organs of action.
manimekalai:27:202-226.reading: The Sankhya speaker says primal nature is hard to know, made of the three qualities, without mind, the common ground from which all things appear; from it in turn appear intellect, space, wind, fire, water, earth, mind and the sense of self, then the senses and their objects from each element and the five organs of action, and from the elements the world of mountains and trees, which returns the way it came into dissolution while primal nature stays one, pervading and eternal.
manimekalai:27:202-226.nuance: The order given (intellect, then the elements, then mind and the sense of self) is not the order of the classical Sankhya texts, where the sense of self comes before the senses and elements; the Tamil account should not be taken as the school's own sequence. No creator is named: nature unfolds and withdraws by itself.

claims.claim: primal nature, made of the three qualities and without mind, is the ground from which all things appear
intellect, the elements, mind, the sense of self, the senses and the organs of action unfold from primal nature in order
the world returns the way it came into dissolution, while primal nature remains one, pervading and eternal

manimekalai:27:227-240.unit_note: Runs from 227, where the account of purusha begins, to 240, which closes the Sankhya section (செப்பிய திறமும் கேட்டு) before the Vaisheshika is addressed at 241.
manimekalai:27:227-240.reading: The Sankhya speaker says the person (purusha) is unlike nature: not of the three qualities, not the ground of things, but the awareness that knows them all, one, pervading and eternal; the principles are twenty-five, the five elements, five sense organs, five objects, five organs of action, mind, intellect, the sense of self, thought, and the soul.
manimekalai:27:227-240.nuance: The count of twenty-five here lists thought (சித்தம்) among the inner organs and ends with the soul, without naming primal nature in the list, so the twenty-five are not quite the classical list. அறிதற்கு எளிதாய் at 227 sets purusha against nature, which was hard to know at 203.

claims.claim: the person is pure awareness, not of the three qualities, one, pervading and eternal
there are twenty-five principles, ending in the soul

manimekalai:27:241-262.unit_note: Runs from 241, where the Vaisheshika is addressed, to 262, where the narrator closes his speech (ஒன்றிய வாதியும் உரைத்தனன்); the core units broke at 261 and 262.
manimekalai:27:241-262.reading: Asked for his doctrine, the Vaisheshika says there are six categories, substance, quality, action, generality, particularity and inherence; substance bears quality and action and is the cause of all compounds, and is ninefold (earth, water, fire, wind, space, direction, time, self, mind); earth has all five qualities and the other elements fewer; and generality is the common being that lets substance and quality act.
manimekalai:27:241-262.nuance: Line 249 gives earth sound among its five qualities; the Vaisheshika's own texts give sound to space alone, so this may be the account's slip or a different count. Lines 257 to 261 on generality are compressed and their sense is tentative.
manimekalai:27:241-262.event: Manimekalai asks the Vaisheshika for his doctrine and he sets it out.

claims.claim: there are six categories: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity and inherence
substance bears quality and action and is ninefold: earth, water, fire, wind, space, direction, time, self and mind
earth has five qualities and the other elements fewer

manimekalai:27:263-276.unit_note: Runs from 263, where the materialist is called on, to 276, which ends his speech (வினை துய்த்தல்'); the core units broke at 275 and 276, mid-sentence.
manimekalai:27:263-276.reading: The materialist says that as intoxication arises when dhataki flowers and jaggery are mixed, awareness arises in the combined elements and is lost when they part, like the sound of a drum dying away; beings with and without awareness both come from the elements; perception alone is valid and inference fails; this life and its fruits are all there is, and a next world where deeds are eaten is a lie.
manimekalai:27:263-276.nuance: The intoxication simile is the materialist's emblem in Tamil polemic: the Jain Neelakesi puts the same image in his mouth. Line 273 makes the materialist's own understanding the measure of truth, which is the point Manimekalai will press.
manimekalai:27:263-276.event: Manimekalai calls on the materialist, and he sets out his doctrine.

claims.claim: awareness arises from the elements combined, as intoxication from mixed ingredients
awareness perishes when the elements separate, like the fading sound of a drum
perception alone is a means of knowledge; inference fails
there is only this life; a next world where deeds bear fruit is false

manimekalai:27:277-283.unit_note: The core unit 276-289 is split: 277 opens with Manimekalai's reply after all the schools, and 283 ends the materialist's rejoinder (ஐயம் அன்றி இல்லை' என்றலும்), before her answer at 283-284 (நின் / தந்தை).
manimekalai:27:277-283.reading: Having heard every path, Manimekalai says that though they are not good she will not answer them, and laughing asks whether there are not those who have come to know a birth before this one; the materialist replies that the minds of those deluded by a god or by dreams are changed, and such knowledge is nothing but doubt.
manimekalai:27:277-283.nuance: The speakers of 278 to 283 are not named and are fixed here from the sense: the laughing question suits Manimekalai, who learnt her own former birth in kaathai 9, and the rejoinder suits the materialist. His answer names the very means of her knowledge: a deity carried her off and she woke at the Buddha's seat.
manimekalai:27:277-283.event: Manimekalai, having heard all the schools, asks the materialist whether no one knows a former birth, and he dismisses such knowledge as delusion.

claims.claim: some have come to know a birth before this one
knowledge of a former birth comes from possession by a god or from dreams, and is mere doubt

manimekalai:27:284-289.unit_note: The last six lines of the core unit 276-289: Manimekalai's answer from 284 (தந்தை தாயரை) to the narrator's close at 289.
manimekalai:27:284-289.reading: Manimekalai answers that he knows his own father and mother only by inference, that without true understanding the true nature of things is hard to know, and that on his terms his own claim can be stated only as doubt; so, speaking in her assumed form, she learned the five kinds of religion.
manimekalai:27:284-289.nuance: The answer turns the materialist's rule on itself: a man who accepts perception alone cannot know his own parents, so his denial of past births is no firmer than the knowledge he calls doubt. The parents example was a fallacy of memory in the logician's list (75 to 77); here it is an inference no one can do without. ஐவகைச் சமயம் counts five where the chapter heard more speakers; which five is not said.
manimekalai:27:284-289.event: Manimekalai refutes the materialist and, having heard them all, comes to know the five kinds of religion.

claims.claim: one knows one's own father and mother only by inference
without true understanding the true nature of things is hard to know

links.note: The logician's perception grasps name, class, quality and action and sits among ten means; Aravanar's Buddhist logic keeps two means and takes name, class, quality and action out of perception.
links.teaches: The epic stages the theory of knowledge as a reply across two kaathais: what the Vedic logician packs into seeing, the Buddhist teacher moves into inference, so the dispute is over where conceptual labels enter knowledge.

links.note: Comparison, scripture, presumption and the rest are independent means for the logician; the Buddhist teacher folds all other means into inference.
links.teaches: Read together, the two lists show the Buddhist reduction is aimed at a named opponent: scripture's unseen worlds lose their standing as a separate source once they must be inferred.

links.note: The logician pairs the Buddhists with சினன் and with two means of knowledge; kaathai 29 has ஆதி சினேந்திரன் teaching exactly two.
links.teaches: The later kaathai confirms that சினன் in the list of schools names the Buddha, so the rival's account of Buddhism here is accurate on the count of means.

links.note: The logician files 'these are your parents', taken on another's word, as a false semblance of knowledge; Manimekalai offers knowing one's parents as an inference no one can refuse.
links.teaches: The chapter's opening list and its closing argument use the same example in opposite ways, so the heroine's rebuttal is also a correction of the logician's classification.

links.note: The Saiva debater defines God as the eight forms; Pattinathar reads the eight forms and Siva's other emblems as teachings, and mocks those who whirl in word and meaning.
links.teaches: Set beside the debate hall, Pattinathar's verse shows the Saiva poets turning the same eight-form creed from a debating thesis into a teaching the arguers fail to grasp.

gains.a: the Saiva's bare list gains a Saiva reading of what each form is meant to teach
gains.b: Pattinathar's scorn for word-proud disputants gains a scene of such disputants at work

links.note: Brahma-vadin, Vaishnava and Saiva each name a different maker or keeper; Tirumular says the three gods are one in continuity and that those who divide them quarrel.
links.teaches: Manimekalai rejects the theistic schools for disagreeing with truth, while Tirumular faults only their division, so the same sectarian quarrel is read as error by the Buddhist and as a misunderstanding by the Saiva.

gains.a: the epic's row of competing creators gains an insider's verdict that they need not compete
gains.b: Tirumular's 'those who divide quarrel' gains a staged instance of the quarrel he condemns

links.note: The Ajivika holds the elemental atoms to be without beginning; Sivavakkiyar says the elements and senses, and even the soul, are not beginningless, and only the truth mingled with them is.
links.teaches: The question of what is beginningless divides the two: for the Ajivika matter itself is eternal, for the Siddhar matter and soul are both made, and only the one truth is without beginning.

gains.a: the Ajivika claim gains a direct contrary from a later Tamil voice using the same word
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's denial gains a named opponent who held the elements beginningless

links.note: The Ajivika says everything a life meets is fixed at conception by prior fate; the Kural says those who strive without flagging see fate's back.
links.teaches: Against the Ajivika's fixed course, the couplet's claim that effort can rout fate stands out as a deliberate limit on oozh, which the Kural elsewhere (380) calls the strongest power.

gains.a: the epic's rival doctrine of total fate gains the Tamil ethical tradition's answer
gains.b: the couplet gains a full statement of the fatalism it resists

links.note: Both end with the two deeds turned back; the Jain does it by blocking new deeds and exhausting old ones, Tirumular by keeping the Lord's feet in mind.
links.teaches: The pair shows Jain and Saiva agreeing that release needs both good and bad deeds stopped, and parting over whether the stopping is one's own labour or follows from holding the Lord.

gains.a: the Jain account gains a Saiva parallel that isolates what is distinctive in its godless method
gains.b: Tirumular's line on the two deeds gains a rival technique for the same end

links.note: The Sankhya speaker has space, wind, fire, water and earth unfold from intellect; Tirumular gives the same chain from மான் (mahat), in his chapter on creation.
links.teaches: The same sequence of elements serves the Sankhya as nature unfolding by itself and Tirumular as part of the Lord's creating, so the cosmology was shared while its cause was disputed.

gains.a: the Sankhya account gains a Tamil Saiva reuse of its sequence
gains.b: Tirumular's uncertain verse gains a fuller statement of the chain it compresses

links.note: The Sankhya speaker counts twenty-five principles with no maker; Tirumular says the Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb.
links.teaches: Tirumular keeps the Sankhya count and adds a maker who shapes the twenty-five for each embryo, which is the step the Sankhya account leaves out.

gains.a: the count of twenty-five gains a later life inside Saiva doctrine
gains.b: Tirumular's twenty-five gains its source in a school that counted them without a god

links.note: The materialist's awareness arising from the elements like intoxication from mixed ingredients appears in the Neelakesi's materialist as well.
links.teaches: Buddhist and Jain polemic both put the liquor simile in the materialist's mouth, which suggests it was the standard Tamil way to state his theory of mind.

links.note: The materialist makes awareness a product of the combined elements; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the dancing self is the five elements and answers with release into open space.
links.teaches: The tension depends on reading Sivavakkiyar's questions as rhetorical denials: the self that sees the house of release is not the elements, against the materialist for whom nothing survives their parting.

gains.a: the materialist's claim gains a Siddhar who puts the same question and answers it the other way
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's question gains the explicit doctrine it rejects

links.note: The materialist calls knowledge of former births the delusion of possession or dream; in kaathai 9 Manimekalai, carried off by the deity in sleep, knew her former birth without error.
links.teaches: The materialist's objection names the very conditions of the heroine's own knowledge, so the epic's story stands as her unspoken answer to him.

links.note: In kaathai 26 she is told to hear each school's doctrine, see it lacks truth, and only then follow the Buddha's way, and she takes an ascetic's form to do so.
links.teaches: The debate chapter carries out a method laid down beforehand: hearing the schools is a prescribed stage of her training, not an open inquiry.

links.note: Here the materialist explains away dream and possession as the mind changed; the Neelakesi's Jain asks him how his elements account for dreams, mantras and omens.
links.teaches: The two epics use dream against the materialist in opposite directions: Manimekalai's opponent uses it to dismiss rebirth, Neelakesi uses it as evidence his elements cannot explain.

links.note: The Kural says the fivefold sense-knowledge is fruitless without true understanding; Manimekalai tells the materialist, who trusts the senses alone, that true things are hard to know without true understanding.
links.teaches: The couplet's general claim becomes a debating move: the heroine uses its contrast between sense-knowledge and true understanding to show that a perception-only rule cannot reach even one's parentage.

gains.a: Manimekalai's rebuttal gains a classical Tamil statement of the same limit on the senses
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete opponent, the materialist, whom its limit refutes

links.note: Having heard the schools in an assumed form, she later tells Aravanar that the five kinds of religion are not right and she has not kept them in mind.
links.teaches: The closing line's 'she learned the five kinds of religion' is completed by her verdict in kaathai 29, which turns the survey into a rejection.

links.note: Manimekalai learns the five kinds of religion on her way to the Buddha's truth; Tirumular says those who saw the six sects did not see him.
links.teaches: Both texts make a survey of the sects a stage to pass through, but Manimekalai's ends in reasoned teaching and Tirumular's in clarity about a Lord the sects miss.

gains.a: the epic's tour of the schools gains a Saiva verdict on the same exercise
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of the sects gains a detailed record of what the sects said

new_concepts.gloss: a means of valid knowledge (pramana): perception, inference and the others the schools count
new_concepts.label_source: The text's word: அளவை வாதி (3), ஒப்புமை அளவை (41), ஆகம அளவை (43), பிரமாண ஆபாசங்கள் and அளவைகள் (57, 77, 85)

new_concepts.gloss: the atom, the indivisible unit of matter in the Ajivika, Jain and Vaisheshika accounts

source_issues: Line 190: the source's line mark reads 227-190, carrying the kaathai number; read as 27-190.
Lines 50, 59, 67, 207-212, 221 and 223 were repaired for the old-font ௌ / ெள confusion (தெளிதல், வெளிப்பட்டு).
Line 36 opens a quotation ("இது மழை பெய்யும்) that is never closed in the text as printed.
Lines 151-152 print பசும்ம், செம்ம், பொன்ன், வெண்ண் with a doubled final consonant, presumably for metre.
Lines 9-12 name what reads as eleven means of knowledge though line 7 implies ten; the descriptions at 14-56 cover ten (மீட்சி ஒழிவறிவு appears to be one item).
Line 184 prints அநித்தயம் for அநித்தியம்; line 90 prints யாக்கையுமய்க்.
